verdict: Avoid new steel re-rolling/TMT exposure in Asansol for now; lend only to branded, integrated re-rollers with verified power and receivables discipline, and decline marginal standalone units.
title: Asansol steel re-rolling & TMT: a note to the credit manager
narrative:
## What this business physically is
A re-rolling mill buys billets or scrap, heats and rolls them into TMT bars, and sells to dealers, builders and government contractors. **Cash is made on the spread between billet cost and TMT realisation, not on volume alone.** Power and fuel are the largest controllable cost, so a unit's real edge is a captive furnace or a fixed-power contract, not a bigger rolling line. Billet is the working-capital sink: inventory sits 20-40 days, dealers take 30-60 days credit, so **every proposal must show how the billet cycle is funded, not just the mill's capacity.** Capex is lumpy and mostly spent before the first sale, so a greenfield mill is a bet on the promoter's balance sheet, not on the TMT market.

## What has changed now
West Bengal's GST collections fell 1.3% Apr-to-date against India's +6.1%, a 7.4 pp gap, and electricity demand grew 5.7% against India's 9.5% [D]. **Both point to weaker local demand and slower offtake in the state, so treat Asansol order books as softer than the national IIP NIC 24 print of +2.4% [D] suggests.** Brent at $113/bbl sits above the $75-100 band [D], which raises freight and power-linked costs for a mill that has no captive generation. Peer results are strong but not local: Steel Exchange India reported ~₹340 crore Q2 FY27 revenue, up ~45% YoY [6], and Rathi Steel crossed ₹200 crore, up over 30% [7]; JSW Steel's Q1 FY27 EBITDA margin was 20% [5]. **Read these as proof that branded, integrated players are winning share, not as evidence that Asansol mills are healthy.** The Vedanta ₹70,000 crore West Bengal exploration with 10,000 jobs envisaged in Asansol [3] is a proposal, not committed capex, so do not lend against it. Local labour tension at DSTPS over 40 contract workers [1] is a reminder that contract-labour disruption can stop a mill.

## Where the growth is
**Pursue branded TMT re-rollers with captive power or a long-term power contract, and dealers tied to government and infrastructure orders.** The peer set shows branded re-bar volumes growing [6][7], and a strong brand commands a premium over market rate [9]. Avoid standalone conversion mills that buy billet on spot and sell to one or two dealers; their margin is the first to vanish when local demand slips [D].

## How to grow safely
Structure term debt against verified capacity utilisation and working capital against a drawing-power limit tied to stock and book debts. **Take monthly stock-and-debt statements, power bills and GST returns; if GST turnover trails bank credits by more than a month, ask for the sales register.** Covenant on gearing and interest cover; a peer at 1.80x gearing [10] shows how fast leverage moves when working capital is debt-funded. For any new mill, check the promoter's equity before disbursement; if it is below the stated project cost, ask for the funding tie-up.

## Early-warning signs
- **Monthly GST vs bank credits:** if the gap widens two months running, freeze fresh limits and inspect stock.
- **Power bill arrears or load cuts:** if a unit misses a bill, ask for the discom notice and reassess.
- **Dealer receivables ageing:** if beyond 60 days rises, cut the drawing power.
- **Billet price spikes:** if input cost jumps without a matching TMT price, ask for the order book.
